# System

->of the<-

## Transcendental
<note>Transcendental: A philosophical term popularized by Immanuel Kant. It refers to the investigation of the mental structures and conditions that make human experience and knowledge possible.</note>

# Idealism
<note>Idealism: The philosophical view that reality is fundamentally shaped by the mind or spirit, rather than being composed solely of independent, material matter.</note>

XIII

Proofs, simply because they are idealistic, would not advance actual knowledge by a single step; for it is well known that a <term>teleological explanation; an explanation based on an object's purpose or "end goal" rather than its physical causes (teleologische Erklärung)</term> of an object can teach me absolutely nothing about its actual origin.

The truths of <term>practical philosophy; the branch of philosophy dealing with ethics, will, and human action (practische Philosophie)</term> can only appear as <note>intermediate links: transitional stages or logical steps within a larger philosophical chain</note> within a system of <term>transcendental idealism; the theory that the mind provides the necessary structure for our experience of reality (transcendentaler Idealismus)</term> itself. What truly falls under the domain of this system from practical philosophy is only its "objective" side—which, in its most general form, is **History**. In a system of idealism, history demands to be <term>transcendentally deduced; logically proven to be a necessary condition of our consciousness (transscendental deducirt)</term> just as much as the "objective of the first order," which is **Nature**. This deduction of history leads simultaneously to the proof that what we regard as the ultimate ground of the harmo— <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page, likely referring to the "harmony" between nature and freedom.</note>

# Introduction.

---

## §. 1.

### The Concept of Transcendental Philosophy.

1. All knowledge is based on the agreement <note>original: "Uebereinſtimmung"</note> of an objective element with a subjective one. — For one knows only that which is true; and truth is generally defined as the agreement of **representations** <note>mental images, thoughts, or perceptions that stand in for objects in the mind (Vorſtellungen)</note> with their **objects**.

2. We may call the sum total of all that is purely objective in our knowledge **nature**; the sum total of all that is subjective, on the other hand, shall be called the **Self** <note>original: "das Ich," often translated in philosophy as the "Ego" or the "I"</note>, or **intelligence**. These two concepts are opposed to one another. Intelligence is originally conceived as that which merely represents <note>the active side of the mind that perceives and thinks</note>, and nature as that which is merely representable; the former as the **conscious**, the latter as the **unconscious**. Now, however, in every...

...knowledge, a mutual meeting of both (the conscious and that which is in itself unconscious) is necessary; the task is: to explain this meeting.

3. In knowledge itself—insofar as I know—the **objective** and the **subjective** are so united that one cannot say which of the two possesses priority. There is no first and no second here; both are simultaneous and one. — In wanting to explain this <term>identity; the state of being exactly the same or a single unity (Identität)</term>, I must have already abolished it <note>The author argues that the very act of thinking about how the mind and the world connect forces us to treat them as separate things, even though in the actual moment of "knowing," they are one single experience.</note>. In order to explain it, since nothing else is given to me besides those two factors of knowledge (as an **explanatory principle**), I must necessarily set one before the other, starting from one in order to arrive at the other; which of the two I start from is not determined by the task.

4. There are therefore only two possible cases.

A. Either the **objective** is made the first, and the question is: how does a **subjective** come to it that corresponds with it?

The concept of the subjective is not contained in the concept of the objective; rather, both mutually exclude each other. The subjective must

<meta>This page continues the first of two philosophical paths described on the previous page: starting from the objective world (Nature) to find the subjective (Intelligence). ...therefore be added to the objective. — It is not contained within the concept of nature that there should also be an **intelligent** being that represents it. Nature, so it seems, would exist even if there were nothing there to represent it <note>The author is using "represent" (vorstellen) in the philosophical sense of a mind perceiving or forming a mental image of the world.</note>. The task can therefore also be expressed thus: How is the **intelligent** added to nature, or how does nature come to be represented?

This task assumes nature or the **objective** as the primary starting point. It is therefore, without doubt, the task of **natural science**, which does the same. — That natural science—even without knowing it—is actually approaching the resolution of that task can only be shown here briefly.

If all knowledge has, as it were, two poles which mutually presuppose and require one another, then they must seek each other in all sciences; there must therefore necessarily be two **fundamental sciences**, and it must be impossible to start from one pole without being driven toward the other. The necessary tendency of all natural science is therefore to move from nature toward the **intelligent**. This, and nothing else, lies at the heart of the effort to bring theory into natural phenomena. — The highest perfection of natural science would be the complete <term>spiritualization; the process of turning material laws into laws of thought or mind (Vergeistigung)</term> of all natural laws...

In the manifestations of magnetism, every material trace already disappears; and of the phenomena of gravitation—which even natural scientists believed they could only understand as a direct spiritual influence—nothing remains but its law, whose execution on a grand scale is the mechanism of celestial motions. — The perfect theory of nature would be that by virtue of which all of nature dissolved into an *intelligence*. — The dead and unconscious products of nature are merely failed attempts by nature to reflect upon itself; so-called dead nature, however, is generally an immature *intelligence*, which is why, though still unconscious, an intelligent character already shines through its phenomena. — The highest goal—to become a complete *object* to itself—nature only reaches through the highest and final reflection, which is nothing other than man, or more generally, what we call <term>reason; the capacity for conscious, logical, and self-reflective thought (Vernunft)</term>,

...the only thing that is (§ 1), it necessarily begins with universal doubt regarding the reality of the **objective**.

Just as the **natural philosopher** <note>original: "Natur-Philosoph"</note>—who is focused only on the objective—seeks to prevent nothing so much as the interference of the **subjective** into their knowledge, so conversely the **transcendental philosopher** seeks to prevent nothing so much as the interference of the objective into the purely subjective principle of knowledge. — The means of exclusion is **absolute skepticism**—not the halfway kind directed only against common human prejudices, which never looks to the foundation, but rather a thorough skepticism that directs itself not against individual prejudices, but against the **fundamental prejudice** <term>Grundvorurtheil; a foundational, instinctive assumption that precedes all other thoughts</term>, with which all others must fall of their own accord. 3) If for the **transcendental philosopher** <note>A philosopher who investigates the mental frameworks that make experience possible, rather than just the objects of experience themselves.</note> only the **subjective** <term>subjective: pertaining to the "I," the self, or the internal mind of the observer</term> possesses original reality, then he will also only make the subjective aspect of knowledge his immediate object. In common, everyday knowledge, the act of knowing itself disappears behind the object being known; however, in transcendental knowledge, the reverse happens: the object as such disappears behind the act of knowing. Transcendental knowledge is thus a **knowledge of knowledge**, insofar as it is purely subjective.

For example, in the case of **intuition** <term>intuition (original: *Anschauung*): the direct, immediate way the mind "sees" or perceives an object, whether through the senses or the intellect</term>, only the objective side reaches our common consciousness; the act of intuiting itself is lost in the object. The nature of the **transcendental way of looking at things** <note>original: *transcendentalen Betrachtungsart*</note> must therefore consist in this: that within it, even those elements which escape our awareness in all other thinking, knowing, or acting—and which are absolutely **non-objective** <note>meaning they do not appear as "things" or "objects" but are part of the hidden process of the mind</note>—are brought to consciousness and made objective. The "transcendental art" will consist precisely in the skill of constantly maintaining oneself in this **duality** <note>original: *Duplicität*</note> of acting and thinking.

It is therefore not a single part, nor a specific object of knowledge, but knowledge itself, and knowledge in general, which it makes its object.

Now, however, all knowledge reduces to certain original convictions, or original **prejudices** <note>original: *Vorurtheile*; in this philosophical context, these are not negative biases but "pre-judgments"—assumptions we hold before we begin to reflect or reason</note>; transcendental philosophy must trace these individual convictions back to a single original conviction. This one, from which all others are derived, is expressed in the **first principle** of this philosophy. The task of finding such a principle means nothing other than finding the **absolutely certain** <note>original: *absolut-Gewisse*</note> through which all other certainty is mediated.

The division of transcendental philosophy itself is determined by those original convictions whose validity it claims. These convictions must first be sought in **common understanding** <note>original: *gemeinen Verstande*; often referred to as "common sense"</note>. According to the *second* conviction, a transition occurs from the world of representation into the real world—meaning the *determination* of the *objective* world by a (*freely designed*) representation within us.

Since the possibility of all free action rests on this prerequisite, the resolution of this task is **practical philosophy**.

It is easy to see that this problem can be resolved neither in theoretical nor in practical philosophy alone. Rather, it must be found in a higher philosophy that serves as the connecting link <note>original: *Mittelglied*; literally a "middle limb" or mediating element</note> between the two—a philosophy that is neither purely theoretical nor purely practical, but both at once.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "pre-established harmony" between the internal world of thought and the external world of objects. It proposes that the fundamental activity of the human spirit is the same whether it is consciously acting or unconsciously creating the world.</meta>

...activity <note>original: *Thätigkeit*; in this philosophical context, this refers to the active force of the mind or the "Self"</note> through which the objective world is produced, is originally identical with the activity that expresses itself in **willing**, and vice versa.

Now, it is certainly a productive activity which expresses itself in willing; all **free action** is productive, but it is productive only with **consciousness**. If we now posit—since both activities are ultimately meant to be one in principle—that the same activity which is consciously productive in free action is *unconsciously* productive in the production of the world, then that pre-established harmony becomes real, and the contradiction is resolved.

If we assume that all this is actually the case, then that original identity—of the activity busy in producing the world with the activity that expresses itself in the will—will represent itself in the products of the former. These products must then appear as products of an activity that is simultaneously **conscious** and **unconscious**.

Nature, both as a whole and in its individual products, must appear as a work brought forth with consciousness, and yet simultaneously as a product of the blindest **mechanism** <term>mechanism: the view that nature operates like a machine according to fixed, non-purposive physical laws</term>; it is purposeful, without being explainable *as* purposeful. — The philosophy of natural ends, or **teleology** <term>teleology: from the Greek *telos* (end or goal); the study of evidence of design or purpose in nature</term>, is therefore that...

<summary>The author argues that the "pre-established harmony" is explained by a single activity that acts consciously during free will and unconsciously when creating the natural world. This explains why nature appears to have a purpose (teleology) while still following blind physical laws (mechanism).</summary>

# Point of Union between Theoretical and Practical Philosophy.

D. So far, we have only generally postulated the identity of that unconscious activity <note>original: *Thätigkeit*; in this philosophical context, the active, creative force of the mind</note> which has brought forth nature, and the conscious activity which expresses itself in willing, without having decided where the principle of that activity lies—whether in nature or in ourselves?

Now, however, the system of knowledge is only to be considered complete when it returns to its own principle. — Transcendental philosophy <term>Transcendental philosophy: a school of thought that examines the mental structures and conditions that make experience and knowledge possible</term> would therefore only be complete if it could demonstrate that **identity**—the ultimate resolution of its entire problem—**within its own principle** (within the "I" <note>original: *Ich*; refers to the conscious Self or the subject of experience</note>).

It is therefore postulated that within the subjective—within consciousness itself—this activity, which is simultaneously conscious and unconscious, must be demonstrated.

Such an activity is the aesthetic alone, and every work of art can only be understood as the product of such an activity. The ideal world of art and the real world of objects are thus products of one and the same activity; the convergence of both (the conscious and the unconscious) without awareness yields the real world, whereas with awareness, it yields the aesthetic world.

### § 4.

## The Organ of Transcendental Philosophy.

1) The only immediate object of transcendental observation is the subjective (§ 2.); the only organ for this manner of philosophizing is therefore the inner sense, and its object is of such a kind that it cannot even become an object of external intuition <note>original: *Anschauung*; in this context, it refers to the direct, immediate perception or "looking upon" an object, rather than a vague "hunch."</note> in the way that mathematics can. — The object of mathematics, to be sure, exists as little outside of knowledge as the object of philosophy. The entire existence of mathematics rests upon intuition; it therefore also exists only within intuition, but this intuition itself is an external one. To this we must add that the mathematician is never immediately concerned with the act of intuition (the construction) itself, but only with the thing constructed, which can indeed be represented externally; meanwhile, the philosopher looks solely at the act of construction <note>original: *Construction*; the mental process of forming a concept or "building" an idea within the mind</note> itself, which is an absolutely internal act.

real knowledge. And conversely, genuine knowledge presupposes a meeting of opposites, a meeting that can only be a **mediated** one.

2) It is assumed as a **hypothesis** <note>original: *Hypotheſe*</note> that there is a **system** in our knowledge; that is, that it is a whole which supports itself and is consistent within itself. — The skeptic <note>original: *Skeptiker*; one who doubts the possibility of certain or absolute knowledge</note> denies this assumption, just as they deny the first, and like the first, it can only be proven through the act itself. — What if our knowledge—indeed, if our entire nature—were self-contradictory? — Thus, assuming only that our knowledge is an original whole, the blueprint of which is to be the system of **philosophy**, we must again ask for the preliminary conditions of such a system.

Since every true system (such as, for example, the structure of the universe <note>original: *Weltbau*; refers to the physical or cosmic order of the world</note>) must have the ground of its existence within itself, it follows that if there is a system of knowledge, its **principle** must lie within knowledge itself.

be. For all truth is absolutely equal to itself. <meta>This page continues the argument for a single, supreme principle of knowledge. There is no talk at all of an absolute *principle* of *being* <note>original: *Princip des Seyns*. In this context, a "principle of being" would be an ultimate cause for why things exist in the physical world (ontology).</note>, for all those objections apply against such a thing, but rather of an absolute *principle* of *knowledge* <note>original: *Princip des Wissens*. This refers to the fundamental rule or starting point for how we think and understand (epistemology).</note>.

Now it is evident, however, that if there were not an absolute *limit* of *knowledge*—something that, even without us being conscious of it, absolutely anchors and binds us in the act of knowing, and which, while we are knowing, does not even become an *object* <note>An "object" here refers to a specific thing we are thinking about; the "principle" cannot be an object because it is the very lens through which we see all objects.</note> for us, precisely because it is the *principle* of all *knowledge*—that then no *knowledge* at all, not even a single instance of it, could ever come about.

The *transcendental philosopher* <term>Transcendental Philosopher: Someone who investigates the internal requirements of the human mind that allow us to experience and understand the world.</term> does not ask what *ultimate ground of our knowledge* might lie *outside of it*, but rather, what is the *ultimate thing within our knowledge itself* beyond which we cannot go? — He seeks the *principle of knowledge within knowledge*; (it is therefore itself something that *can be known*).

The assertion that there is a *highest principle of knowledge* is not like the assertion that there is an *absolute principle of being*; it is not a *positive* claim, but a *negative, limiting assertion*, which implies only this: *there is some ultimate point from which all knowledge begins, and beyond which there is no knowledge*.

<meta>This page transitions from the general necessity of a starting point for knowledge to identifying that specific starting point. Since the **transcendental philosopher** <term>Transcendental Philosopher: A thinker who investigates the internal mental structures and conditions that make human experience and knowledge possible.</term> (Intro § 1) everywhere makes only the *subjective* <note>In this context, "the subjective" refers to the internal workings of the mind and the act of thinking, rather than the external things we think about.</note> into his *object*, he also maintains only that it is subjective—that is, that there is for us some kind of **first knowledge**. Whether there exists anything at all beyond this first knowledge, abstracted from us, does not concern him for now; the subsequent findings must decide that later.

This first knowledge for us is, without a doubt, the knowledge of ourselves, or **self-consciousness**. When the **idealist** <note>An idealist is a philosopher who believes that reality as we know it is fundamentally constructed by the mind or "ideas," rather than existing independently of our perception.</note> makes this knowledge the principle of philosophy, it is in accordance with the limited scope of his entire task, which has nothing as its object except for the subjective aspect of knowledge. — That self-consciousness is the fixed point to which everything is tied for us needs no proof. — But whether this self-consciousness itself might only be the modification of a higher *being* — (perhaps of a higher consciousness, and this of one higher still, and so on into infinity) — in a word, whether even self-consciousness might still be something generally explainable, explainable from something of which we can know nothing, because it is only through self-consciousness that the entire **synthesis** <term>Synthesis: The mental process of combining different perceptions or concepts into a single, unified thought or experience.</term> of our knowledge is first made — this is of no concern to us as transcendental philosophers; for to us, self-consciousness is not a kind of *being* <note>original: *Seyn*. Here, the author distinguishes between "Being" (existence as a thing-in-itself) and "Knowing" (how we perceive and understand).</note>, but a kind of *knowing*, and indeed the highest and outermost that exists for us at all.

--- Page 47 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the starting point of philosophy. While the previous page established self-consciousness as the starting point for the internal (subjective) perspective, this page argues that even if we try to start with the external (objective) world, we are inevitably led back to self-consciousness to make sense of it.</meta>

It can even be proven, going further—and has already been partially proven above (Intro. § 1)—that even if the **objective** <note>The "objective" refers to the world of external things and matter, viewed as existing independently of our thoughts.</note> is arbitrarily set as the primary starting point, we still never get beyond **self-consciousness**. In our explanations, we would then either be driven back into infinity—from the consequence to its ground—or we would have to arbitrarily break the chain by positing an **Absolute** <note>The "Absolute" refers to a final, ultimate reality that needs no further explanation because it is the cause of itself.</note> that is its own cause and effect—**subject** and **object**. Since this is originally only possible through self-consciousness, we would once again be setting self-consciousness as the primary thing. This is what happens in **natural science**, for which **being** <term>Being (Seyn): The simple state of existing as a thing, which some philosophers wrongly assume is the most basic starting point of reality.</term> is just as little a primary starting point as it is for **transcendental philosophy** (see the *Outline of a System of Natural Philosophy*, p. 5). Natural science places the only real reality in an Absolute that is its own cause and effect—in the **absolute identity** of the **subjective** and **objective**, which we call **Nature**, and which at its highest power is again nothing other than self-consciousness.

**Dogmatism** <note>In this era, "dogmatism" referred to philosophical systems (like those of Spinoza) that assumed external objects are more real than the thinking mind.</note>, for which **being** is the primary thing, can generally only explain things through an infinite regress <note>An "infinite regress" is a logical failure where every answer requires a new "why," leading back forever without ever reaching a final foundation.</note>; for the chain of causes and effects through which its explanation proceeds could only be [grounded] by something that is simultaneously the cause and effect of itself—

<meta>This page concludes the argument from the previous page regarding the necessity of a foundational point for human knowledge. ...necessarily be a point where synthetic knowledge arises from the identical, and the identical from the synthetic.

6) To be able to solve the task of finding such a point, we must without doubt delve even deeper into the opposition between **identical** and **synthetic** propositions.

In every proposition, two concepts are compared with one another; that is, they are set as either equal or unequal to one another. In the **identical proposition** <note>original: "identiſchen Satze"; a statement where the predicate is already contained in the subject, like "a square has four sides."</note>, however, **thought is merely compared with itself**. — The **synthetic proposition** <note>original: "ſynthetiſche Satz"; a statement that adds new information not already contained in the definition of the subject, like "the square is made of wood."</note>, on the other hand, goes beyond mere thought; by thinking the **subject** <term>Subject: In logic, the part of a statement that the statement is about.</term> of the proposition, I do not also automatically think the **predicate** <term>Predicate: The part of a statement that says something about the subject.</term>; the predicate is added to the subject. The **object** is therefore not merely determined by being thought here; it is regarded as **real**, for that which is **real** is precisely what cannot be created through mere thought.

If, then, an **identical proposition** is one where the concept is compared only with the concept, and a **synthetic** one is where the concept is compared with an object distinct from it, then the task—to find a point where identical knowledge is simultaneously synthetic—is equivalent to: **finding a point in which the object and its concept, the thing and its representation, are originally, absolutely, and without any mediation, one.**

That this task is identical to the task of finding a principle of all knowledge can be demonstrated even more briefly as follows. — How a **representation** <note>original: "Vorstellung"; the mental image or concept we have of a thing, as opposed to the thing itself.</note> and an **object** can coincide is absolutely inexplicable, unless there is a point within knowledge itself where both are originally one — or where the most perfect identity of **being** and **representing** exists.

7) Since representation is the subjective, while being is the objective, the task, defined most precisely, amounts to this: to find the point where subject and object are **immediately** <note>original: "unvermittelt"; meaning "without mediation" or without any intervening steps or logical gaps.</note> one.

8) Through this ever-closer narrowing of the task, it is now as good as solved. — That immediate identity of subject and object can only exist where that which is **represented** is at the same time the **representer**, and that which is **observed** <note>original: "Angeschaute"; often translated in philosophy as "intuited," referring to the direct perception of something.</note> is also the **observer**. — But this identity of the represented with the representer is found only in **self-consciousness**; thus, the sought-after point is found in self-consciousness.

**Intellectual intuition is the organ of all transcendental thinking.** <note>Transcendental thinking refers to a philosophy that investigates the underlying conditions of our experience—not just *what* we know, but *how* it is possible for us to know anything at all.</note> For transcendental thinking aims precisely at making itself into an Object through freedom—an object that is otherwise not an object at all; it presupposes a capacity to simultaneously produce and intuit <note>original: "anzuſchauen"; to "intuit" here means to perceive or "see" something directly with the mind's eye without needing a logical argument.</note> certain acts of the spirit, so that the production of the Object and the intuition itself are absolutely one. Since Reinhold set the scientific foundation of philosophy as his goal, there has been much talk of a **first principle** from which philosophy must proceed; this was generally understood to be a **theorem** <note>original: *Lehrsatz*; a formal statement or proposition that can be proven.</note> in which the whole of philosophy was supposed to be contained. A **theorem** is a proposition that concerns an **existence** <note>original: *Daseyn*; referring to something that already exists "out there" in the world.</note>. **Transcendental philosophy**, however, does not proceed from any existence, but rather from a **free action**, and such an action can only be **postulated**. Every science that is not empirical <note>Empirical sciences rely on observation of the external world.</note> must, through its first principle, already exclude all empiricism; that is, it must not presuppose its object as already present, but must **produce** it. 

This is how **geometry** proceeds, for example, by proceeding not from theorems but from **postulates**. Because the most original construction in geometry is **postulated**, and it is left to the student himself to produce it, he is directed toward **self-construction** <term>self-construction|German: *Selbstconstruction*; the process by which the mind activey builds a concept rather than passively receiving it.</term> right from the beginning. — The same is true for **transcendental philosophy**. Without already bringing the transcendental mode of thought with one, one must find it incomprehensible. k) The proposition I = I simultaneously fulfills the second requirement placed upon the principle of knowledge: that it ground both the form and the content of knowledge. # Second Main Section.

## General Deduction of Transcendental Idealism.

---

### Preliminary Remark.

1. Idealism is already expressed in our first <term>principle</term>. <note>original: "Grundsatze." A foundational proposition or axiom upon which a system of thought is built.</note> Because the **I** <note>original: "Ich." In German philosophy of this period, the "Ich" (often translated as the Ego) refers to the self-conscious subject or the mind as the starting point of experience.</note> also *is* [exists] immediately through its being thought—for it is nothing other than the act of thinking itself—the proposition **I = I** is identical to the proposition: **I am**. This stands in contrast to the proposition **A = A**, which only says: *if* A is <term>posited</term>, <note>original: "gesetzt." In this context, to posit something means to place it in the mind as an object of thought or to assert its existence.</note> it is posited as equal to itself. The question—"is it actually posited?"—is not even possible regarding the **I**. Now, if the proposition **I am** is the principle of all philosophy, then there can be no reality other than that which is equal to the reality of this proposition. But this proposition does not say that I exist for anything outside of me, but only that **I exist for myself**. Therefore, everything that exists at all will only be able to exist **for the I**; there will be no other reality at all.

From this mutual presupposition of both activities for the sake of self-consciousness, the entire mechanism of the Self will be derived.

**Realism.** If I reflect only on the **ideal activity**, then **Idealism** arises for me—or the assertion that the **boundary** is set solely by the **Self**. <note>In this context, "Idealism" suggests that the external world and its limits are products of our own minds.</note> If I reflect only on the **real activity**, then **Realism** arises for me—or the assertion that the **boundary** exists independently of the **Self**. gg) In ***theoretical philosophy***, the **ideality** of the boundary is explained (or: how **limitedness**, which originally exists only for **free acting**, becomes limitedness for **knowledge**?); ***practical philosophy*** has to explain the **reality** of the boundary (or: how limitedness, which is originally merely subjective, becomes **objective**?). <note> "Theoretical philosophy" refers to how we know things (epistemology), while "practical philosophy" refers to how we act in the world (ethics/agency).</note> Therefore, ***theoretical philosophy*** is ***idealism***, ***practical*** is ***realism***, and only both together constitute the completed system of ***transcendental idealism***.

Just as ***idealism*** and ***realism*** mutually presuppose one another, so too do ***theoretical*** and ***practical philosophy***; and in the ***Self*** itself, that which we must separate for the purpose of the ***system*** currently being established is originally one and united.

# I.

## Deduction of the absolute synthesis contained in the act of self-consciousness.

1. We proceed from the proposition proven in the preceding section: the **limit** <term>Schranke: In this context, a boundary or restriction that defines the "I" by separating it from everything else.</term> must be simultaneously **ideal** <term>Ideal: Relating to ideas, thoughts, or the mind’s internal activity.</term> and **real** <term>Real: Relating to objective existence or things as they are in the world.</term>. 2. But such an act is only **self-consciousness**; therefore, all **limitedness** <note>The state of having boundaries or being a finite individual.</note> must first be established through self-consciousness and be given alongside self-consciousness.

Self-consciousness, in its principle, is merely ideal; but through this very act, the **"I"** <term>Ich: The "Self" or "Ego"; the conscious subject that says "I."</term> arises for us as something purely real. As certainly as the "I" is conscious of itself, so certainly must that conflict arise and be maintained. The question is: how is it maintained?

Two opposing directions cancel each other out, they destroy one another; thus, it seems, the conflict cannot endure. From this, absolute **inactivity** would arise, for since the "I" is nothing but a striving to be equal to itself, the only determining reason for **activity** for the "I" is a persistent **contradiction** <note>The author argues that if our minds were perfectly at peace with no internal friction, we would have no reason to think or act at all.</note> within itself. Now, however, every contradiction in and of itself destroys itself. No contradiction can exist, except perhaps through the very endeavor to maintain it, or to think it; through this third element itself, a kind of **identity**, a reciprocal relationship between the two opposing members, enters into it.

against the **Subject** <note>original: "Subject". If the opposition were not an absolute one, the unifying activity would likewise not be absolute, necessary, or involuntary <note>original: "unwillkührlich." This suggests the mind's unifying process happens automatically or spontaneously, rather than by a conscious choice.</note>.

**Reality**, for the very reason that it is absolute, is not "reality" <note>original: "Realität." In this philosophical context, "reality" refers to something limited and defined that we can perceive. If something is "absolute" (infinite and without limits), it cannot be a discrete reality in our everyday experience.</note>; therefore, both opposites in this state of opposition are merely ideal. If the **I** <term>The I (das Ich): The fundamental self, the conscious subject, or the "knower."</term> is to become real—that is, to become an **Object** <note>The Object is that which is perceived or thought about—the "known."</note> to itself—then reality must be sublated within it; that is, it must cease to be absolute reality. But likewise: if the opposite is to become real, it must cease to be absolute negation. If both are to become real, they must, so to speak, share reality between themselves. However, this division of reality between the two—the subjective and the objective—is only possible through a third activity of the **I** hovering between both; and this third activity is, in turn, not possible unless both opposites themselves are activities of the **I**.

This progression from **thesis** to **antithesis** and from there to **synthesis** <term>Synthesis: The third stage of thought where a conflict between a proposition (thesis) and its opposite (antithesis) is resolved into a higher unity.</term> is thus originally grounded in the **mechanism of the spirit** <note>original: "Mechanismus des Geistes." This refers to the structural, involuntary way the human mind generates thought and experience.</note>. Insofar as this progression is merely formal (for example, in scientific method), it is an abstraction from that original, material progression established by **transcendental philosophy** <term>Transcendental Philosophy: A branch of philosophy that investigates the necessary internal conditions that allow for human experience and knowledge.</term>.

4) The **real activity** <note>The "real" activity is the aspect of the mind that interacts with the external world and encounters resistance, creating the sense of physical reality.</note> is thus limited by the derived **mechanism** <term>Mechanism: in this context, the automatic or law-governed processes of nature and the mind that function without conscious choice</term>, but without this yet being the case for the *Self* itself. Following the *method* of theoretical *philosophy*—which is to *deduce* <note>To logically trace the origin or necessity of something.</note> for the **ideal Self** what is posited in the **real Self** (for the observer)—the entire investigation turns to the question of how the real *Self* can also be limited for the ideal *Self*. At this *point*, the task stands: to explain how the *Self* comes to **view itself** <term>Intuition/Viewing: from "anschauen," the mind's act of immediate perception or "looking at" its own state.</term> as limited.

a) The real, now limited activity is to be posited as an activity of the *Self*; that is, a ground of *identity* <note>A reason why the two distinct things—the mind and the action—can be considered the same.</note> between it and the *Self* must be demonstrated. Since this activity is to be ascribed to the *Self*, and yet simultaneously distinguished from it, a ground of distinction between the two must also be shown.

What we call the *Self* here is merely the ideal activity. The ground for relating and distinguishing must therefore be sought in one of the two activities. However, the ground for relating and distinguishing always lies in that which is related; now, since the ideal activity is here simultaneously the relating activity, the ground must be sought in the real activity.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the conflict between the Self's two primary activities: the "real" activity (which interacts with the world) and the "ideal" activity (which reflects upon itself). On the previous page, the author argued that if these activities remained in perfect balance, the Self would be like "dead matter." The ground of distinction between both activities is the **limit** <term>Gräntze (Limit): A boundary or constraint that defines the scope of the mind's power.</term> set within the **real activity**, for the **ideal** is that which is simply unlimitable, while the **real** is now the limited one. The ground of relation between the two must likewise be sought in the real; that is, something ideal must be contained within the real itself. The question is: how is this conceivable? Both are merely distinguishable through the limit, for even the opposing directions of both are only distinguishable through the limit. If the limit is not set, there is within the **Self** <term>Ich (Self): The fundamental "I" or conscious subject.</term> mere identity, in which nothing can be distinguished. Once the limit is set, there are two activities within it: the limiting and the limited, the subjective and the objective. Both activities thus have at least one thing in common: that originally they are both absolutely non-objective; that is, because we do not yet know any other character of the ideal, both are equally ideal.

b) This being presupposed, we can conclude further in the following way:

The ideal activity, which until now was unlimited, is the infinite **tendency** <note>The inherent drive or direction of the mind's power.</note> of the Self to become an **object** to itself in the real activity. By virtue of that which is ideal in the real activity (which is what makes it an activity of the Self in the first place), it can be related to the ideal activity, and the Self can **intuit** <term>Intuition: Translated from "Anschauung," referring to the mind's immediate "viewing" or grasping of an object or itself.</term> itself within it (this is the first "becoming-an-object-to-oneself" of the Self).

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the self (the I) encounters the external world. It distinguishes between the "positive" aspects of objects, which the mind can actively construct, and the "accidental" limitations that seem foreign or "inconstructible" to our reason.</meta>

The <term>accidental<note>original: Accidentelle; in philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential or contingent properties of a thing (like its color or size) rather than its essential nature</note></term> (everything that belongs to <term>limitation<note>original: Begräntztheit; the state of being finite or bounded</note></term>) must appear to us as the <term>inconstructible<note>original: Inconſtructible; that which the mind cannot create or explain through pure reason alone</note></term>, something inexplicable from the <term>I<note>original: Ich; the self-conscious subject or the ego</note></term>, whereas the "positive" element of things can be understood as a <term>construction<note>the mind’s active process of organizing and "building" its experience of the world</note></term> of the I. However, the proposition that the I (our object of study) finds itself limited by an <term>opposite<note>original: Entgegengeſetztes; also translated as the "Not-I," or the external world that stands against the self</note></term> is qualified by the fact that the I nevertheless finds this opposite only *within* itself.

It is not claimed that there is something in the I that is *absolutely* opposite to it, but rather that the I *finds* something in itself *as* something absolutely opposite to it. To say the opposite is "in the I" would mean it is absolutely opposed to the I; but to say the I *finds* something as opposed to itself means it is only opposite in relation to its act of <term>finding<note>original: Finden; the process of discovery or sensing</note></term> and the specific way this finding occurs—and that is indeed the case.

That which "finds" is the <term>infinite tendency<note>original: unendliche Tendenz; the fundamental drive or striving of consciousness to expand and know itself</note></term> to <term>intuit<note>original: anzuſchauen; to behold or perceive directly with the mind’s eye</note></term> itself, in which the I is purely <term>ideal<note>existing as a concept or mental act</note></term> and absolutely unlimitable. That *in which* the finding occurs is not the pure I, but the <term>affected I<note>original: afficirte Ich; the self when it is being acted upon by sensations</note></term>. Therefore, the "finder" and "that in which it finds" are themselves opposites. Whatever exists within the "found" appears to the "finder" as something foreign—but only insofar as it functions as the finder.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the "I" (the Self) perceives the world. It concludes the sentence from the previous page regarding the "infinite tendency" of the self toward self-awareness, explaining that what we perceive as external objects are actually just moments where our own internal activity has been interrupted or "negated."</meta>

...toward <term>self-intuition<note>original: Selbstanſchauung; the act of the mind looking at itself or becoming its own object of study</note></term>, the <term>I<note>original: Ich; the conscious subject or the self</note></term> finds within itself as the "intuited" object—or, what is the same thing (since in this act the one looking and the one being looked at are not distinguished)—something foreign to itself. But what is this thing that is "found" (or sensed) during this process of finding? That which is sensed is, after all, only the I itself. Everything sensed is an immediate presence, something absolutely unmediated; this is inherent in the very concept of sensation. The I certainly finds an <term>opposite<note>original: Entgegengeſetztes; that which stands against the self, often referred to as the "Not-I"</note></term>, but it finds this opposite only within itself. However, in the I there is nothing but <term>activity<note>original: Thätigkeit; the active, productive power of the mind that constitutes our reality</note></term>; therefore, nothing can be opposed to the I except for the <term>negation<note>original: Negation; the absence or stopping of a positive force</note></term> of activity. To say that the I finds an opposite within itself means, therefore, that it finds within itself its own **suspended activity**. — Whenever we have a sensation, we never sense the "object" itself; no sensation provides us with a concept of an object. In fact, sensation is the absolute opposite of a <term>concept<note>original: Begriff; the mental "grasping" or understanding of something through active thought</note></term> (which is an action); sensation is therefore the negation of activity. The logical jump from this negation to an external object as its cause is a much later step, the reasons for which can once again be found within the I itself.

Since the I only ever senses its own suspended activity, the thing sensed is not actually different from the I; the I is only sensing itself. Common philosophical language has already expressed this by calling the thing sensed something "merely subjective."

This is a system that would have to be desirable to the philosopher, if only it actually delivered what it promises. 

Yet, in the form materialism has taken until now, it is completely incomprehensible; and as soon as it becomes comprehensible, it is actually no longer different from **transcendental idealism**. — To explain **thinking** as a material phenomenon is only possible by turning matter itself into a ghost, into a mere modification of an **intelligence**, of which thinking and matter are joint functions. Consequently, materialism itself is driven back to the **intelligent** as the original source. 

Of course, it is just as impossible to explain **Being** through **knowledge** in such a way that the former is the effect of the latter; no relationship of causality is possible between the two at all, and both can never meet unless they are originally **One**, as they are in the **I**. **Being** (matter) considered as productive is a **knowledge**; **knowledge** considered as a product is a **Being**. ->Two questions immediately arise here:<-

a) What does it actually mean to say: the **boundary** <note>original: *Gräntze*; a limit or restriction encountered by the mind.</note> is determined through **ideal activity** <note>original: *ideelle Thätigkeit*; the mind's internal capacity to think and perceive, as opposed to external physical action.</note>?

Of the **boundary**, nothing remains in **consciousness** <note>original: *Bewusstseyn*.</note> now except the trace of an absolute **passivity** <note>original: *Passivität*; the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression from the outside.</note>. Since the **Self** <note>original: *Ich*; the conscious subject or "I".</note> does not become conscious of the act within the **sensation** <note>original: *Empfinden*.</note>, only the result remains. This **passivity** is, up to this point, completely indeterminate. But **passivity** in general is as little thinkable as limitedness in general. All **passivity** is a *specific* <note>original: *bestimmte*; literally "determined" or "definite."</note> one, just as surely as it is only possible through the negation of **activity**. The **boundary** would therefore be determined if the **passivity** were determined.

That mere **passivity** is the mere matter of **sensation** <note>original: *Empfindung*.</note>, that which is purely felt. The **passivity** would be determined if the **Self** gave it a specific sphere—a specific **sphere of influence** <note>original: *Wirkungskreis*; literally "circle of effect," referring to the range or domain within which something operates.</note> (if one will permit this figurative expression here). The **Self** would then be passive only within this sphere, and active outside of it.

That act of determining would therefore be a **producing** <note>original: *Produciren*; the creative act of the mind forming a concept.</note>; the matter of this **producing** would be the original **passivity**.

### b) How this act of production itself might be conceived?

The **Self** <note>original: *Ich*; the conscious subject or the "I."</note> cannot produce the **sphere** <note>original: *Sphäre*; the domain or range of experience.</note> without being **active** <note>original: *thätig*.</note>, but it can just as little produce the sphere as a sphere of **limitedness** <note>original: *Begräntztheit*; the state of having boundaries or being finite.</note> without being limited itself in the process. — Insofar as the Self is the thing that limits, it is active; but insofar as it is the limiter of its own limitedness, it itself becomes something limited.

That act of **producing** <note>original: *Produciren*; the mind's internal process of generating its own experience or objects of thought.</note> is thus the most absolute union of **activity** and **passivity**. The Self is passive in this act, for it cannot determine the limitedness without already presupposing it. But conversely, even the **ideal Self** <note>the mind as a thinking subject, rather than a physical being.</note> is limited here only insofar as it aims to determine that limitedness. In that act, there is thus an activity which presupposes a **passive state** <note>original: *Leiden*; literally "suffering," but used here in the philosophical sense of being the recipient of an action, the opposite of "doing."</note>, and conversely, a passive state which presupposes activity.

Before we reflect again upon this union of passivity and activity within a single act, we can see what we would have gained through such an act if it could indeed be demonstrated to exist within the Self.

In the preceding moment of consciousness, the Self was only **something felt for itself**. <note>original: *Empfundenes für sich*; the Self as an object of its own internal sensation rather than a thinking agent.</note>

And so it is. The derived **action** is an act of **producing**. In this producing, the **ideal Self** <note>the thinking subject in its pure, active state</note> is now completely free. It is, therefore, only a boundary between the Self and its opposite, the <term>thing-in-itself</term> <note>original: *Ding an sich*; a famous philosophical term for reality as it exists independently of our senses and thoughts</note>. Consequently, through this action—if only the possibility of the action itself were comprehensible—that opposition between the Self and the thing-in-itself (in short, everything that previously had been established only for the **philosopher**) would also be **deduced** <note>logically proven or derived from first principles</note> for the Self itself.

## II.

We certainly see from this entire discussion that the given **solution** to the problem is undoubtedly the correct one, but this solution itself is not yet fully comprehensible, and we are likely still missing some connecting links.

<summary>The author argues that while the mind creates its field of experience, the boundaries of that field must come from an external "thing-in-itself." This provides a logical bridge between the internal subject and the external world.</summary>

--- Page 158 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the Self's activity and passivity. The author identifies a logical paradox—an "insoluble circle"—where sensing requires the Self to be both active and passive simultaneously, a contradiction that requires further breakdown to truly understand how the mind perceives its own limits.</meta>

It was shown through this resolution that the **ideal Self** <note>the mind as a perceiving or thinking subject</note> cannot become passive without already having been active. Thus, a mere impression upon the ideal (intuiting) Self can in no way explain **sensation** <note>original: *Empfindung*; the raw feeling of an external stimulus</note>. It also became clear that the ideal Self, in turn, cannot be active in a specific way without already being passive. In a word, it was shown that in that action, **activity** and **passivity** <note>original: *Activität* and *Paſſivität*; the state of doing versus being done to</note> mutually presuppose one another.

Now, the final act through which sensation is fully established within the Self might indeed be of this nature, but there must still be **intermediate links** between this act and the original sensation. This is because, with that act, we already find ourselves placed in that **insoluble circle** <note>a logical loop where two things depend on each other for their own existence</note> which has always plagued philosophers. If we wish to remain faithful to our current path, we must first allow this circle to arise before our very eyes in order to fully comprehend it ourselves.

By what, then, is the thing limited? By the same boundary through which the Self is also limited. As many degrees of activity in the Self, just as many degrees of non-activity in the thing, and vice versa. # Theory of Productive Intuition.

### Preliminary Remark.

**Descartes** <note>original: *Cartesius*; the Latinized name for the French philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650)</note> said as a physicist: give me matter and motion, and I will construct the universe for you out of them. The Transcendental Philosopher <term>Transcendental Philosopher</term> <note>A philosopher following the tradition of Kant and Fichte, who seeks to understand the underlying structures of the mind that make experience possible</note> says: give me a nature composed of opposing activities—one that reaches toward the infinite, and another that strives to behold itself within this infinity—and I will show you how intelligence, with its entire system of ideas, arises from them. Every other science assumes that intelligence is already fully formed; the philosopher, however, observes it in the process of becoming, and allows it to emerge, as it were, before their very eyes.

The **Self** <term>Self</term> <note>original: *Ich*; the "I" or the conscious subject</note> is merely the ground upon which intelligence, with all its determinations, is applied. The original act of self-consciousness explains to us only how the **Self** exists in regard to its objective activity—in its primal striving—but not how it [enters] <note>The German text ends on the prefix "ein-", likely part of a word like *eintritt* (enters/occurs)</note> into its subjective nature or into knowledge...

## Second Epoch.

### From productive intuition to reflection.

### Preliminary Remarks.

The first epoch concludes with the elevation of the <term>Self</term> <note>original: "Ich." In German Idealism, this refers to the conscious subject or the fundamental "I" that experiences the world.</note> to <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: "Intelligenz." This describes a being that is not just active, but aware of its own mental processes.</note>. The two activities, which were completely separated and located in entirely different spheres, are merged back into one and the same product through the intervention of a third activity. Through this intervention of a third activity into both, the activity of the thing also becomes once again an activity of the Self, which is thereby itself elevated to intelligence.

But the Self, while it is engaged in <term>intuition</term> <note>original: "Anschauung." <meta>This page continues the logical derivation of the principle of causality. We derive the **relationship of causality** <term>causality</term> <note>The principle that every effect has a cause; here, it is viewed as a necessary structure of the mind to organize experience.</note> as the necessary condition under which alone the **I** <note>original: "Ich." The conscious self or subject.</note> can recognize the present **Object** as an object. If a **representation** <note>original: "Vorstellung." A philosophical term for the variety or "multiplicity" of data received by the senses.</note> of representations (this follows naturally), but even the present object would not be recognized as "present."

The **succession** <note>The following of one thing after another in time.</note> within the relationship of causality is a necessary one. In an original sense, no arbitrary succession in our representations is even conceivable. The "choice" or arbitrariness which occurs, for example, when we perceive the individual parts of a whole as an **organic** entity or a **work of art** <note>original: "Kunstproduct."</note>, is ultimately itself grounded in a relationship of causality. Regardless of which part of an organism I begin with, I am always driven from one part to the other, and from that one back again, because in anything organic, everything is **reciprocal cause and effect** <term>reciprocal interaction</term> <note>original: "Wechselwirkung." A state where two things act upon each other simultaneously.</note>. Of course, this is not the case with a work of art; here, no single part is the "cause" of the other, yet one still presupposes the other within the productive understanding of the artist. This holds true everywhere that succession in our representations otherwise seems arbitrary—for instance, in the perception of the individual parts of inorganic nature, in which there is likewise a general interaction of all parts.

<summary>The author argues that causality is the essential mental framework that allows us to perceive objects in time. While we derived the series of productions through which the **Self** <term>Ich (The "I"): The core subject or ego that experiences and acts.</term> gradually reached the point of viewing itself as productive, no **activity** <term>Thätigkeit: The active power or energy of the mind.</term> appeared through which the **intelligence** <term>Intelligenz: The self-aware mind or conscious subject.</term> completely tore itself away from producing altogether. However, the way each derived "product" was placed into the intelligence's own **consciousness** <term>Bewuſstseyn: The state of being aware of oneself and the world.</term> could only be explained by a constant **reflecting** <term>Reflectiren: The act of the mind turning its attention back upon its own internal processes.</term> of the mind upon what it had produced. The only problem was that through every act of reflection, a condition for a brand-new act of producing arose.

In order to explain this forward progress in producing, we had to attribute an activity to our **object** <term>Object: In this context, the "Self" that we are observing as it develops consciousness.</term> by virtue of which it strives to go beyond each individual act of producing; yet, through this very striving, it constantly entangled itself in new productions. We can therefore know in advance that the series of actions we have now postulated belongs generally to the sphere of **reflection**.

## Third Epoch.

### From Reflection to the Absolute Act of Will.

->I.<-

In the series of synthetic acts <term>Synthetische Handlungen: Mental processes where the mind combines different elements to create a new, unified understanding.</term> derived thus far, none could be found through which the *Self* <term>Ich: The "I" or the conscious subject; the fundamental starting point of this philosophical system.</term> would have immediately arrived at the consciousness of its own activity. It is the process by which the mind links an abstract, universal rule (like the idea of a "circle") to a specific, sensory image (a round shape seen in the world).</term>, which each person can only come to know through their own internal experience, and which one, in order to make it recognizable and to guide that experience—

The **schema** <term>Schema: In Kantian philosophy, a mental bridge or "pattern" that allows an abstract concept (like "dog") to be applied to a sensory image (a specific furry animal).</term> must be distinguished both from the **image** and from the **symbol**, with which it is very frequently confused. It is **intuition** <term>Anschauung (Intuition): The mind's ability to "see" or grasp something directly through the senses or the imagination, rather than through abstract logic.</term>, and thus not a **concept**, for it is that which mediates between the concept and the object. But it is also not the intuition of the object itself, but only the intuition of the rule according to which such an object can be produced.

## II.

Now, however, in the original **mechanism** of **intuition** <note>original: "Anschauung"; the mind's immediate, direct perception of an object before it even thinks about it.</note>, no **object** actually appears as **possible** or **impossible**, whereas every object *does* appear as **substance** and **accident** <term>Substance and Accident: "Substance" is the underlying thing that stays the same, while "accidents" are its changing properties (like a chair being painted a new color).</term>. **Objects** appear as **possible**, **actual**, and **necessary** only through the **highest act of reflection**, which up to this point has not even been derived. They express a mere relationship of the **object** to the entire **faculty of knowledge** (**inner** and **outer sense**), such that neither through the concept of **possibility**, nor even through that of **actuality**, is any specific **determination** or quality placed within the **object** itself. That relationship of the **object** to the entire **faculty of knowledge** is, without doubt, only **possible** once the **I** <note>original: "Ich"; the conscious self or the subject.</note> has completely torn itself away from the **object**—that is, from its own **ideal** and **real activity** simultaneously—which is to say, only through the **highest act of reflection**. In relation to this act, the **categories** of **modality** can then be called the **highest**, just as those of **relation** are the highest in regard to the **synthesis** of **productive**...

### III.

**Transcendental abstraction** <term>Transcendental Abstraction: The mental process of separating a general concept from the specific sensory details of an object.</term> is the condition for **judgment**, but not the **judgment** itself. It explains only how the **intelligence** <note>original: "Intelligenz"; the active, thinking faculty of the mind.</note> comes to separate the **object** and the **concept**, but not how it reunites them both in **judgment**. How the **concept**, which in itself is entirely devoid of **intuition**, reconnects with the **intuition** of **space**—which in itself is entirely devoid of **concepts**—to form an **object** is unthinkable without a **mediating element**. But that which mediates between the **concept** and **intuition** in general is the **schema**. Thus, **transcendental abstraction** will be resolved once more through a **schematism** <term>Schematism: A conceptual "bridge" that allows our abstract thoughts to link up with our sensory perceptions.</term>, which we shall call the **transcendental** one, to distinguish it from the one derived earlier.

The **empirical schema** was explained as the sensibly intuited rule according to which an **object** can be **empirically** produced. The **transcendental** schema, therefore, will be the sensible **intuition** of the rule according to which an **object** in general, or **transcendental**, can be produced. Now, insofar as the **schema** contains a rule, it is only the **object** of an **inner intuition**; insofar as it is the rule for the **construction** <term>Construction: The mind's active process of "building" or mapping out a concept in space and time, such as drawing a triangle in one's mind.</term> of a...

But the most original thing that mediates between the **inner** and **outer sense** is **time**—not insofar as it is merely **inner sense**, i.e., an **absolute limit** <note>original: "abſolute Gräntze"; here meaning a boundary that defines the internal sequence of thoughts.</note>, but insofar as it itself becomes once more an **object** of **outer intuition** <term>Intuition: In this philosophical context, "intuition" (Anschauung) refers to the mind's immediate, direct perception of something in time or space, before any conscious reasoning happens.</term>; that is, **time** insofar as it is a **line**, i.e., a magnitude extended in a single direction.

Viewed from the standpoint of **reflection**, **time** is originally only a **form of intuition** of the **inner sense**, since it occurs only in respect to the **succession** <note>original: "Succeſſion"; the following of one thought after another.</note> of our **representations** <note>original: "Vorſtellungen"; the mental images or "objects" present in the mind.</note>, which from this standpoint is merely within us; whereas we can only intuit the **coexistence** <note>original: "Zugleichſeyn"</note> of **substances**—which is the condition of both **inner** and **outer sense**—outside of ourselves. ## IV.

Transcendental abstraction was postulated as the condition for empirical abstraction, and the latter as the condition for **judgment** <note>original: *Urtheil*. In this philosophical context, judgment is the mental act of applying a concept to a specific thing (e.g., "This rose is red").</note>. Underlying every judgment, even the most common, is that abstraction; and the transcendental faculty of abstraction—or the faculty of concepts *a priori*—is as necessary in every intelligence as self-consciousness itself.

# General Remark on the Third Epoch.
<note>In this context, an "Epoch" refers to a specific stage or period in the history of the mind’s self-development as it moves toward full self-awareness.</note>

The final investigation that must conclude the whole of theoretical philosophy is, without doubt, the one regarding the difference between concepts *a priori* <note>original: *a priori*. This is, of course, only possible because it transports itself into a region lying beyond common consciousness. In contrast, a philosophy that restricts itself to the latter can only find these concepts as already present and, as it were, lying there—a situation that entangles it in the insoluble difficulties that have always been leveled against the defenders of these concepts.

# Fourth Main Section.

## System of Practical Philosophy according to the Principles of Transcendental Idealism.

---

It seems appropriate to remind readers beforehand that what we intend to present here is not a **moral philosophy** <term>Moral-Philosophie: A system of ethical rules or a guide on how to live.</term> itself, but rather the **transcendental deduction** <term>Deduction: In this context, a logical proof that explains the origin of a concept, showing why it is valid and how it is possible in our minds.</term> of the very **thinkability** and **explainability** of **moral concepts** <note>original: "moralischen Begriffe." These are the foundational ideas of ethics, such as duty, will, and freedom.</note> in general. Furthermore, we will conduct this investigation into those parts of moral philosophy that belong to **transcendental philosophy** <term>Transcendental Philosophy: The study of the internal structures of our mind that make experience and knowledge possible.</term> with the utmost generality. In this way, we will reduce the whole to a few main propositions and problems, while leaving the application to individual cases to the reader. By doing so, the reader can most easily discover if they have not only grasped **transcendental idealism** <note>original: "transcendentalen Idealismus." The philosophical view that our experience of the world is shaped by the necessary structures of our own minds.</note>, but—and this is the most important thing—whether they have also learned to use this method of philosophy as an **instrument of investigation**.

### First Proposition. Absolute Abstraction.

<summary>This section introduces the "Practical Philosophy" part of the system, clarifying that it focuses on the logical foundations of moral concepts rather than providing a list of ethical rules. It encourages the reader to use transcendental idealism as a practical tool for their own philosophical inquiries.</summary>
<keywords>practical philosophy, moral concepts, transcendental deduction, transcendental idealism, philosophical method, absolute abstraction</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "First Proposition" concerning "Absolute Abstraction," moving from the definition of the concept to a proof of how the mind initiates consciousness through self-governance rather than external cause.</meta>

That is, the **beginning of consciousness** is only explainable from a **self-determination**, or an **act of the intelligence** <term>Intelligence: In this philosophical context, "intelligence" does not mean cleverness, but the active, thinking mind or the capacity for self-awareness.</term> upon itself.

**Proof.** What is understood by absolute abstraction is assumed to be known. It is the act by virtue of which the **intelligence** absolutely raises itself above the **objective** <term>Objective: The "objective" refers to the world of things and objects as they exist outside or apart from our thinking self.</term>. Since this act is an absolute one, it cannot be conditioned by any of the preceding acts; with this act, therefore, the connection of actions—in which each subsequent action is made necessary by the preceding one—is, as it were, broken, and a new series begins.

To say an action does not follow from a previous one of the intelligence means: it is not explainable from the intelligence insofar as it is **this** specific intelligence, or insofar as it acts **in a specific way**; and since it must be explainable at all, it can only be explained from the **absolute in the intelligence itself**, from the ultimate **principle of all acting** <note>original: "Princip alles Handelns." This refers to the fundamental source or ground of human agency.</note> within it.

That an action is only explainable from the ultimate ground in the intelligence itself must (since the ultimate ground in the intelligence is nothing other than its original **duplicity** <term>Duplicity: The inherent "two-fold" nature of the mind, where it is simultaneously the subject that thinks and the object being thought about.</term>) mean the same as: the intelligence must determine itself to this action—

## Corollaries.

1) That self-determining of the intelligence is called **willing** in the most general sense of the word. That in every act of **willing** there is a **self-determining**, or that it at least appears as such, everyone can prove to themselves through inner intuition; whether this appearance is true or deceptive does not concern us here. Nor are we speaking here of a specific instance of willing in which the concept of an object would already be present, but rather of **transcendental self-determination**, of the **original act of freedom**. What that self-determination actually is, however, cannot be explained to anyone who does not know it from their own **intuition** <term>Intuition: Translated from the German "Anschauung," meaning a direct, immediate mental "viewing" or internal experience that does not rely on external senses or logical deduction.</term>.

For this contradiction, a mediating concept must be found—a concept that has not occurred to us at all thus far in the sphere of our knowledge. In resolving this problem, we shall proceed as we have with others: namely, by defining the task more and more precisely until only the single possible resolution remains.

To say that an action of the intelligence is **unexplainable** means that it does not arise from any preceding action. Since we currently know of no other type of mental action besides **producing** <note>In this philosophical context, "producing" refers to the mind’s active process of creating its own thoughts and experiences.</note>, this means the action cannot be explained by any preceding act of production by the intelligence. The statement "the action is unexplainable from an act of production" does not mean the action is absolutely unexplainable. However, since there is nothing at all in the intelligence except what it produces, then that "something"—if it is not a production—cannot be *within* it. Yet, it *must* be within it, since an action occurring in the intelligence is to be explained by it. The action is therefore to be explainable from something that

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into the origins of self-awareness and freedom. ...with it freedom first arises; how can a free **non-acting** <note>German: *Nichthandeln*; a state of passive potential or restraint that exists before a choice is made.</note> be conceived of prior to freedom?

These three problems must be resolved above all else, before we can proceed further in our investigation.

**Resolution of the first problem.** Through the **act** <note>German: *Act*; a specific mental deed or event.</note> of **self-determination** <note>German: *Selbstbestimmung*; the capacity of the mind to define its own state.</note>, I am to arise to myself as an "I", that is, as a **Subject-Object** <note>German: *Subject-Object*; a core concept in German Idealism where the self is simultaneously the observer (subject) and the thing being observed (object).</note>. Furthermore, that act is to be a free one; the ground of my determining myself must lie solely and exclusively within me. If that action is a free action, then I must have **willed** that which arises for me through this action, and it must arise only because I willed it. Now, however, that which arises for me through this action is **willing** <note>German: *Wollen*; the power of the will. In this philosophy, the "I" does not just *have* a will, it *is* an act of willing.</note> itself (for the "I" is an original willing). I must, therefore, have already willed this willing before I can act freely; and yet, the concept of willing arises for me—along with that of the "I"—only through that very action.

This obvious **circle** <note>German: *Cirkel*; a logical paradox or "catch-22" where the conclusion is required to establish the premise.</note> can only be resolved if "willing" can become an object for me prior to the actual act of willing. This is impossible through my own power alone; therefore, it would have to be that very concept of willing that arises for me through the action of an **intelligence** <note>German: *Intelligenz*; in this context, it refers to another conscious, rational being or mind.</note>.

This question has already been largely answered by our previous discussion.

Not only does individuality involve **existence** <note>original: *Daſeyn*</note> at a specific point in time, along with other limitations imposed by our **organic existence** <term>organic existence: Life as a biological, physical entity with a body that exists in space and time.</term>, but individuality is also further limited through the very act of **acting** itself. As we act, our individuality is restricted anew, in such a way that one could say, in a certain sense, the individual becomes less and less free the more they act. <note>The author suggests that every choice we make "locks in" a specific path, thereby reducing the infinite possibilities we had before we acted.</note>

However, it is impossible for these other intelligences to prevent me from wanting *several* different things; therefore, the ultimate reason why I choose object C out of the various possible objects B, C, or D must lie within myself alone. Now, this reason cannot lie in my **freedom** <note>original: *Freyheit*</note> itself, because it is only through this limitation of my free activity to one specific object—

# E.

## Task:

->To explain how **Willing** <note>original: "das Wollen." The active faculty of choice or volition.</note> becomes objective for the **Self** <note>original: "dem Ich." The conscious subject.</note> once again.<-

## Resolution.

### I.

**Third Proposition.** Willing is originally and necessarily directed toward an external **Object**.

**Proof.** Through the free act of **self-determination**, the Self, as it were, annihilates all "matter" of its representation, in that it makes itself completely free in regard to the objective world; it is only through this act that "willing" actually becomes "willing." However, the Self could not become conscious of this act as such unless this willing became an object for it once again. This is only possible if an object of **intuition** <term>intuition: (German: "Anschauung") In this philosophical context, the direct, immediate perception or "looking at" an object in the mind's eye.</term> becomes a visible expression of that willing. Yet, every object of intuition is a specific, definite one; it would therefore have to be *this* specific one, only because and
