insofar as the *Self* <note>original: "das Ich." The conscious subject or the "I."</note> would have willed in this specific way. Through this alone would the *Self* become the self-cause of the *matter* <note>original: "Materie." In this context, the raw content or "stuff" of a thought or perception.</note> of its representation.

But furthermore, the *act*, through which the *object* becomes this specific one, must not be absolutely identical with the *object* itself; otherwise, the *act* would be a blind *production*, a mere *intuition* <term>intuition: (German: "Anschauen") The immediate, direct perception of something, like seeing an object before you have a word for it.</term>. The *act* as such and the *object* must therefore remain distinguishable. Now, however, the *act* conceived as such is a *concept*. That the *concept* and the *object* remain distinguishable is only possible because the *object* exists independently of this *act*—that is, because the *object* is an *external* one. — Conversely, it is for this very reason that the *object* becomes an *external* one to me only through *willing*, for *willing* is *willing* only insofar as it is directed toward something independent of itself.

Here it is already explained—and will be explained even more fully in what follows—why the *Self* simply cannot appear to itself as producing an *object* in its *substance* <note>original: "Substanz." The essential material or "thing-in-itself" that makes up the object.</note>, but rather why all *production* in *willing* appears only as a *shaping* or *forming* of the *object*.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Self" (the I) and the mental activity required to bridge the gap between abstract thought and physical action. It specifically explores the role of the imagination as the mediator between reason and the understanding.</meta>

For this very reason, the **power of imagination** <term>power of imagination: (German: "Einbildungskraft") Here, it is described not just as a creative faculty, but as the mental force that holds opposing thoughts in balance.</term> is not **understanding** in that state of hovering, but rather **reason**; and conversely, what is commonly called **theoretical reason** is nothing other than the **imagination** in the service of **freedom**. However, that **Ideas** <term>Ideas: (German: "Ideen") In this philosophical tradition, Ideas are concepts of the infinite (like the soul or the universe) that cannot be fully grasped by the senses.</term> are mere objects of the **imagination**—which find their existence only in that hovering between **finitude** and **infinity**—is clear from the fact that, when made into objects of the **understanding**, they lead to those insoluble contradictions which **Kant** <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), the philosopher who famously identified the "Antinomies," or contradictions, that arise when reason tries to understand the nature of the universe as a whole.</note> set forth under the name of the **Antinomies of Reason**. The existence of these contradictions rests solely on the fact that either one reflects upon the **object**, in which case it is necessarily **finite**, or one reflects again upon the **reflection** itself, whereby the object immediately becomes **infinite** once more. 

Now, since it is obvious that if the question of whether the object of an **Idea** is finite or infinite depends merely on the free direction of **reflection**, then the object itself cannot be one or the other in its own right. Thus, those **Ideas** must indeed be mere products of the **imagination**—that is, of an **activity** that produces neither the **finite** nor the **infinite**.

But in every feeling, a **contradiction** is felt, and indeed nothing can be felt at all except an inner contradiction within ourselves. Through every contradiction, the condition for activity is now immediately given; the activity arises as soon as its condition is given, without any further reflection. If this is at the same time a **free activity**—which, for example, **production** <note>In this context, "production" likely refers to the mind's automatic, unconscious creation of mental images, which is not considered a "free" act of will.</note> is not—it is for that very reason, and only insofar, a **drive**.

## II.

Before we can answer this question, however, another stands in our way. We can only provide the main points for the answer to this question, as it appears here primarily as a connecting link in the investigation. — To be sure, the **pure will** <term>reiner Wille: the part of the mind that acts based on reason and moral duty, rather than physical cravings</term> cannot become an object for the **I** <term>Ich: the conscious subject or the "Self"</term> without simultaneously having an external object. But now, in the concept of **happiness** <term>Glückseligkeit: a state of harmony where the external world matches our internal desires or will</term>, when it is precisely analyzed, nothing is thought other than the very identity of that which is independent of willing with the willing itself. Thus, happiness—the object of the **natural drive** <term>Naturtrieb: the innate impulse to satisfy our physical needs and find satisfaction in nature</term>—is meant to be only the appearance of the pure will; that is, it is one and the same object as the pure will itself. Both are meant to be absolutely one, so that no **synthetic relationship** <term>synthetisches Verhältniſs: a connection between two distinct things, like a cause and an effect</term> between them—such as between that which **conditions** and that which is **conditioned**—is possible; but also, so that neither can exist independently of the other. If happiness is understood as something that is possible independently of the pure will, then there shall simply be no such thing. But if happiness is only the identity of the external world with the pure will, then both are one and the same object, only viewed from different sides.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the legal framework (the "second nature") must operate with the same mechanical necessity as the physical world. It explains why law must remain separate from morality to avoid the dangers of personal whim or "despotism."</meta>

It is to be viewed like a **machine** <note>original: "Maschine"</note> that is set up in advance for certain cases and acts of its own accord—that is, completely blindly—as soon as these cases arise; and although this machine was built and set up by human hands, it must, as soon as the artisan withdraws his hand, continue to operate according to its own laws, just like visible nature, and remain as independent as if it existed through itself.

## Solution.

### I.

1. All acting is only to be understood through an original union of **freedom** and **necessity**. The proof is that every action—both that of the individual and that of the entire species—must be thought of as **free** insofar as it is acting, but as an **objective result** it must be thought of as standing under **laws of nature**. Subjectively, therefore, for the purpose of inner appearance, we act; objectively, however, we never act, but rather something else acts, as it were, through us.

2) This objective element which acts through me is now, however, supposed to be "I" once again. Yet, I am only that which is **conscious**; that other element, by contrast, is the **unconscious**. Therefore, the unconscious in my acting is supposed to be identical with the conscious. Now, however, this identity in free act- <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the page concludes; it likely continues on the following page to explain how this identity is realized in a free action.</note>

# Fifth Main Section

## Fundamental Principles of Teleology according to the Principles of Transcendental Idealism

---

Just as certainly as the appearance of freedom can only be understood through a single, identical activity <note>original: "Thätigkeit". In this philosophical system, activity refers to the fundamental power of the mind or spirit to act and create.</note> which, for the sole purpose of appearing, has divided itself into conscious and unconscious parts, so too must nature—as that which is produced without freedom—appear as a product that is **purposive** <note>original: "zweckmäfsig". This describes something that looks like it was designed for a specific goal or end, even if no designer is visible.</note>, without having been produced according to a purpose. That is to say, nature must appear as a product that, although it is the work of a blind **mechanism** <term>Mechanism: The physical laws of cause and effect that operate automatically, like a machine, without any internal thought or intention.</term>, nonetheless looks as if it were produced with consciousness.

# Sixth Main Section.

## Deduction of a General Organ of Philosophy, or: Fundamental Principles of the Philosophy of Art according to the Principles of Transcendental Idealism.

---

### §. 1.

### Deduction of the Work of Art in General.

The postulated **intuition** <term>Intuition: A translation of the German "Anschauung," referring to a direct, immediate mental "seeing" or grasp of an object, rather than through step-by-step reasoning.</term> is intended to unify what exists separately in the appearance of **freedom** <note>Meaning conscious human action and choice.</note> and in the intuition of the **product of nature** <note>Meaning the unconscious, automatic processes of the natural world.</note>; namely, the identity of the conscious and the unconscious within the **Self** <term>Self: The "I" (Ich), the active subject of consciousness.</term>, and the consciousness of this identity. The product of this intuition will therefore border on the product of nature on one hand, and the product of freedom on the other, and must unite the characteristics of both within itself. If we know the product of this intuition, then we also know the intuition itself; we therefore only need to derive <note>In philosophy, "to derive" (deducieren) means to logically trace a concept back to its necessary origins or first principles.</note> the product in order to derive the intuition.

The product will have in common with the product of freedom that it is produced with consciousness—

### § 2

### Character of the Product of Art.

a) The work of art reflects back to us the identity of conscious and unconscious activity. Yet the opposition between these two is an infinite one, and it is resolved without any contribution from freedom <note>The author means that this resolution happens naturally or instinctively through the creative act, rather than through a conscious act of will or moral choice.</note>. Thus, the fundamental character of the work of art is an **unconscious infinity**.

Beyond what the artist has placed into the work with clear intention, he seems to have instinctively represented an infinity, which no finite intellect is capable of fully unfolding. To clarify this with just one example: Greek mythology—of which it is undeniable that it contains an infinite meaning and symbols for all ideas—emerged among a people and in a manner that makes it impossible to assume a consistent intentionality in its invention, nor in the harmony with which everything is united into one great whole <note>The author suggests that Greek myths are too complex and meaningful to have been "invented" by a single person or intentional group; they must have grown from an unconscious, collective cultural spirit.</note>. It is the same with every true work of art; each one, as if an infinity of intentions [were present]...

However, it could very easily be proven in various ways that these reasons for suspicion can also be highly deceptive.

Genius is distinguished from everything else that is merely **talent** or **skill** <term>Skill (*Geschicklichkeit*): The learned ability to perform a task or create something through rules and practice, as opposed to the innate, spontaneous power of genius.</term> by the fact that it resolves a **contradiction** <term>Contradiction (*Widerspruch*): A fundamental philosophical conflict; here, Schelling refers to the tension between the artist's conscious intent and the unconscious forces of nature or inspiration.</term> that is absolute and otherwise unsolvable by any other means. In everything—even the most common and mundane production—an unconscious activity works together with the conscious one; but only a production whose condition was an **infinite opposition** <term>Opposition (*Gegensatz*): The polar tension between the artist's subjective will and the objective necessity of the creative process.</term> of both activities is an **aesthetic** one, and possible only through genius—

## General Note on the Whole System

If the reader, having followed our path attentively to this point, reflects once more upon the connection of the whole, they will undoubtedly make the following observations:

That the entire system falls between two **extremes**, one of which is designated by **intellectual intuition**, the other by **aesthetic intuition**. What <term>intellectual intuition</term> <note>original: *intellectuelle Anschauung*. This refers to the philosopher's ability to "see" the internal activity of the mind as it happens.</note> is for the philosopher, <term>aesthetic intuition</term> <note>original: *ästhetische Anschauung*. This refers to the way we perceive a work of art as a physical object that perfectly expresses a spiritual idea.</note> is for their **object**. The first, since it is necessary merely for the sake of the particular direction of the spirit which the philosopher adopts while philosophizing, does not occur in common consciousness at all; the other, since it is nothing other than intellectual intuition which has become universally valid or objective, can at least occur in every consciousness. 

It can also be seen from this very fact, however, that and why philosophy, as philosophy, can never become universally valid. The one thing to which **absolute objectivity** is granted is **Art**. Take away, one might say, objectivity from art, and—

He argues that while philosophy remains an elite activity of the mind, art serves as the universally accessible bridge where these internal thoughts become objective reality.</summary>

# E r r a t a .

---

Page 4. Line 4. Lawful. <note>original: "Gesetzmässige"</note>
— 10. — 12. Read "it" instead of "he." <note>original: "es" instead of "er"</note>
— 46. — 6 from the bottom. Instead of "Act" read "Kind." <term>Kind <gloss>Art</gloss>: A correction from "Act" (action) to "Art" (type or nature).</term>
— 72. — 7 from the bottom. Read "I." <note>original: "I c h"</note>
— 78. — 11 from the bottom. Read "but" instead of "taber." <note>A correction of a simple typo.</note>
— 100. Before Line 9. There must be a 1).
— 116. Line 7 from the bottom. The comma after "self" must stand before this word.
— 136. — 4. Read "perceived." <note>original: "empfundenen"</note>
— — — 6. "inhibited" instead of "inhibited." <note>A grammatical correction of the adjective ending from "gehemmten" to "gehemmte."</note>
— 143. — 17. Before "than a," a comma.
— 146. — 8 from the bottom. Read "Sensation." <term>Sensation <gloss>Empfindens</gloss>: Refers to the act of feeling or perceiving.</term>
— 212. — 2. "in" instead of "in the." <note>original: "in" instead of "im"</note>
— 220. — 2 from the bottom. "second" instead of "Second." <note>A correction from a capitalized noun-form to a lowercase adjective.</note>
— 222. — 10 from the bottom. "reciprocal" instead of "—ge." <note>Correcting the word "wechselseitig" which was likely truncated or misspelled in the original printing.</note>
— 227. — 11 from the bottom. Instead of "C. on. B." read "B — C."
— 293. — 10 from the bottom. Read "can." <note>original: "kann"</note>
— 358. — 8. Read "Products." <note>original: "Producte"</note>
— 378. — 5 from the bottom. "occurs in action." <note>original: "im Handeln vorkommt"</note>
